steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on improving vision-language alignment in CLIP-style encoders by adding multi-tag classification on objects and attributes parsed from captions. Cover the coarse-alignment problem, prior tag-based work, our method, and the headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Goal of V&L encoders and the coarse-alignment problem
- Supervised annotated data: helps, but doesn't scale
- Automatic parsing / tag-based methods and their gaps
- Our approach: LLM-parsed tags + multi-tag classification loss
- Attribute supervision and what it shows

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- V&L encoders (e.g., CLIP)
  - key: extract semantically aligned info from visual and linguistic data
  - well-aligned encoder: versatile; text-to-image generation quality, multi-modality understanding
  - problem: coarse alignment; vision encoder struggles to localize attribute-specified object (Fig. 1); hard to localize arbitrary concepts
- Supervised data with manual annotations
  - mask, bounding box, category; SA-1B, OpenImages, JFT300M
  - critical for precise localization of arbitrary categories
  - but: data gathering, sampling, human annotation effort -> limits scalability, generalization
- Automatic parsing of image-text pairs
  - NLTK de-facto in V&L field; tags from captions; helps but noisy -> limits upper bound of perceiving semantic concepts
  - Tag2Text: universal, unified label system + data annotation engine; about 4,000 tags from image-text datasets (e.g., CC12M)
  - RAM series: image-tag recognition with decoder module; classifies commonly human-used categories
  - DiHT: distills extra multi-tag classifier (private tags) only into CLIP visual encoder
  - these improve visual classification, don't explicitly explore vision-language alignment
  - open question: how to use multi-tags to align image and text embeddings
  - two questions: number of tags (limited tags -> potential not unleashed); how to use various tags (attributes, objects)
- Our approach
  - embarrassingly simple; no extra data formats beyond image-text pairs
  - parse objects (e.g., cat) and attributes (e.g., brown) from description; likely in image
  - parsing by large language model: high-end, fully automatic -> quality, scalability
  - multi-tag classification loss complements image-text contrastive loss
  - localizes text-specified (attribute-specified) objects -> more precise alignment
  - results (Fig. 2): 10 semantic segmentation datasets, average 5.2% improvement
  - only CC12M with parsed text as training set -> efficient and effective
- Attribute information
  - strong open-vocabulary semantic segmentation; flexible to add attributes
  - Fig. 1: attribute supervision -> CLIP localizes 'brown cat'
  - different tag types can enhance different aspects of cross-modal alignment

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
A key aspect when learning vision-language (V&L) encoders like CLIP is to extract semantically aligned information from both the visual and the linguistic data in an effective way. A well-aligned vision-language encoder is remarkably versatile, which includes unprecedented quality in text-to-image generation and also improvements in multi-modality understanding tasks. But existing attempts usually have a problem of coarse alignment, e.g., the vision encoder has trouble localizing an attribute-specified object (as shown in Fig. 1), so it is hard to precisely localize arbitrary concepts.

To get more precise multi-modality alignment, various methods use large-scale supervised data with manual annotations. Some supervised data (i.e., mask, bounding box, or category) like SA-1B, OpenImages and JFT300M has been shown to be critical for improving precise localization of arbitrary categories. Performance improves for commonly used categories, but using such annotated datasets needs rigorous effort in data gathering, sampling and human annotation, and this limits their scalability and generalization.

- Automatic parsing of image-text pairs
  - NLTK de-facto in V&L field; tags from captions; helps but noisy -> limits upper bound
  - Tag2Text: unified label system + annotation engine; about 4,000 tags (e.g., CC12M)
  - RAM series: image-tag recognition with decoder module, commonly human-used categories
  - DiHT: distills multi-tag classifier (private tags) only into CLIP visual encoder
  - all focus on visual classification, not V&L alignment
  - open question: multi-tags for image-text embedding alignment; two questions: number of tags, how to use various tags (attributes, objects)
- Our approach
  - simple; only image-text pairs; LLM parses objects (cat) and attributes (brown)
  - multi-tag classification loss + image-text contrastive loss
  - localizes attribute-specified objects -> more precise alignment
  - 10 semantic segmentation datasets, average 5.2% improvement (Fig. 2); trained only on CC12M with parsed text
- Attribute information
  - flexible to add attributes; Fig. 1: 'brown cat'
  - different tag types -> different aspects of cross-modal alignment

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A key aspect when learning vision-language (V&L) encoders like CLIP is to extract semantically aligned information from both the visual and the linguistic data in an effective way. A well-aligned vision-language encoder is remarkably versatile, which includes unprecedented quality in text-to-image generation and also improvements in multi-modality understanding tasks. But existing attempts usually have a problem of coarse alignment, e.g., the vision encoder has trouble localizing an attribute-specified object (as shown in Fig. 1), so it is hard to precisely localize arbitrary concepts.

To get more precise multi-modality alignment, various methods use large-scale supervised data with manual annotations. Some supervised data (i.e., mask, bounding box, or category) like SA-1B, OpenImages and JFT300M has been shown to be critical for improving precise localization of arbitrary categories. Performance improves for commonly used categories, but using such annotated datasets needs rigorous effort in data gathering, sampling and human annotation, and this limits their scalability and generalization.

So recently researchers have looked at how to automatically parse the data of image-text pairs, especially the text. The automatic text parsing tool NLTK has become a de-facto approach in the V&L field, and it can generate some tags from the caption of an image. These tags can improve the performance of V&L models, but they bring in a lot of noise from NLTK, which may stop the models from reaching the upper limit of accurately perceiving semantic concepts. To collect higher-quality data, Tag2Text designs a universal and unified label system with an efficient data annotation engine, which generates about 4,000 tags from some image-text datasets (e.g., CC12M). Based on these tags, the RAM series of works explore an image-tag recognition system with a decoder module that can classify commonly human-used categories. Also, DiHT distills the knowledge from an extra multi-tag classification model, which is trained on collected private tags, only into the visual encoder of CLIP. These methods focus on improving the classification performance of visual encoders, and they don't explicitly explore the alignment between vision and language. So there is a core question still worth exploring: how can various multi-tags be used to help the alignment between the image and text embeddings from V&L encoders? I argue that there are two important questions in the training design of multi-modal encoders based on multi-tags. The first one is the impact of the number of tags. Even with high-end tag signals in prior methods, a limited number of tags means they fail to fully unleash the potential of multiple tags. The second one is that there is not enough comprehensive exploration of how to effectively use various tags (e.g., attributes and objects).

In this paper we propose an embarrassingly simple approach to improve the alignment between image and text features, which doesn't need any additional data formats beyond image-text pairs. Given an image and its paired text, we automatically parse objects (e.g., cat) and attributes (e.g., brown) from the description, which very likely exist in the image. This parsing pipeline is done by a large language model, which is high-end and fully automatic, so quality and scalability are ensured. We use these parsed semantics as supervision signals, and so we can complement the commonly used image-text contrastive loss with a multi-tag classification loss, which lets the model better capture the visual semantic concepts that the texts refer to. This way our method can accurately localize text-specified objects (e.g., an attribute-specified object), and the alignment between image and text is more precise. Extensive experimental results, shown in Fig. 2, on a broad suite of semantic segmentation datasets (10 datasets) show an average 5.2% improvement of our framework over existing alternatives. Also, we only use the CC12M dataset with the parsed text as the training set, which shows that our method is both efficient and effective.

Besides the remarkable performance on open-vocabulary semantic segmentation tasks, our method is also very flexible for incorporating attribute information. The visualization results in Fig. 1 show that with attribute supervision CLIP can accurately localize the attribute-specified object ('brown cat'). This means that different types of tag supervision could enhance the cross-modal alignment ability of CLIP in different aspects.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A key aspect in learning vision-language (V&L) encoders, e.g., CLIP [1], is to effectively extract semantically aligned information from both visual and linguistic data. A well-aligned vision-language encoder stands out for its remarkable versatility, which includes unprecedented quality in text-to-image generation as well as improvements in multi-modality understanding tasks. However, existing attempts usually face the problem of coarse alignment, e.g., the vision encoder struggles to localize an attribute-specified object (as depicted in Fig. 1), making precise localization of arbitrary concepts hard to achieve.

To improve precise multi-modality alignment, various methods draw support from large-scale supervised data with manual annotations. Specifically, supervised data (i.e., mask, bounding box, or category) such as SA-1B [2], OpenImages [3], and JFT300M [4] has been proven critical for improving precise localization of arbitrary categories. Despite the performance improvements observed in commonly used categories, utilizing such annotated datasets necessitates rigorous efforts in data gathering, sampling, and human annotation, which limits their scalability and generalization.

Thereupon, researchers have recently turned their attention to automatically parsing the data of image-text pairs, especially the text. Concretely, the automatic text parsing tool NLTK has become a de-facto approach in the V&L field, generating tags from the caption of an image. While these tags can bring performance improvements to V&L models, they incorporate much noise from NLTK, which may restrict the models’ ability to reach the upper limit of accurately perceiving semantic concepts. To collect higher-quality data, Tag2Text [5] designs a universal and unified label system with an efficient data annotation engine, generating about 4,000 tags from image-text datasets (e.g., CC12M). Based on these tags, the RAM series of works [5,6] explores an image-tag recognition system with a decoder module that can classify commonly human-used categories. Additionally, DiHT [7] distills the knowledge from an extra multi-tag classification model, trained on collected private tags, only into the visual encoder of CLIP. These methods focus on improving the classification performance of visual encoders without explicitly exploring the alignment between vision and language. A core question is still worth exploring: how can various multi-tags be utilized to help the alignment between the image and text embeddings from V&L encoders? I argue that there are two important questions in the training design of multi-modal encoders based on multi-tags. The first concerns the impact of the number of tags: even with high-end tag signals, a limited number of tags makes prior methods fail to fully unleash the potential of multiple tags. The second is the lack of comprehensive exploration of how to effectively utilize various tags (e.g., attributes and objects).

In this paper, we propose an embarrassingly simple approach to improve the alignment between image and text features without the need for additional data formats beyond image-text pairs. Specifically, given an image and its paired text, we automatically parse objects (e.g., cat) and attributes (e.g., brown) from the description, which are highly likely to exist in the image. This parsing pipeline is implemented by a large language model, which is high-end and fully automatic, ensuring quality and scalability. Using these parsed semantics as supervision signals, we complement the commonly used image-text contrastive loss with a multi-tag classification loss, enabling the model to better capture the visual semantic concepts referred to in the texts. As a result, our method can accurately localize text-specified objects (e.g., attribute-specified objects), achieving more precise alignment between image and text. Extensive experimental results on a broad suite of semantic segmentation datasets (10 datasets), shown in Fig. 2, substantiate an average 5.2% improvement of our framework over existing alternatives. Moreover, we only use the CC12M dataset with the parsed text as the training set, indicating that our method is both efficient and effective.

Besides its remarkable performance on open-vocabulary semantic segmentation tasks, TaskAlign also enjoys high flexibility in incorporating attribute information. The visualization results in Fig. 1 show that the inclusion of attribute supervision enables CLIP to accurately localize the attribute-specified object (‘brown cat’). This finding indicates that different types of tag supervision have the potential to enhance CLIP's cross-modal alignment ability in different aspects.
